  - No physical exam findings (hepatosplenomegaly, dehydration, signs of sepsis).
  - No maternal/newborn blood types or direct antiglobulin test (Coombs) to exclude immune hemolysis.
  - No peripheral smear, hemolysis markers (LDH, bilirubin fractionation confirmed indirect), or G6PD consideration if indicated by ethnicity.
  - No maternal medication history (some meds may cause breast‑milk jaundice).
- Therefore current information is insufficient to conclusively diagnose breast‑milk jaundice and to safely exclude other important causes or determine need for treatment.

4. Physical exam findings: hydration status, hepatomegaly/splenomegaly, signs of illness/sepsis.
5. Maternal and neonate blood types and direct antiglobulin (DAT/Coombs) test.
6. Peripheral smear and hemolysis labs (if hemolysis suspected): reticulocyte count (numeric), LDH, peripheral smear; consider G6PD testing if indicated.
7. Maternal medication history (including any drugs taken postpartum).
8. If any concern for conjugated cholestasis (even though current direct is low): obtain LFTs and consider fractionated bilirubin confirmation and evaluation for biliary atresia if stools persistently pale.

Collecting these items will allow safe differentiation between breast‑milk jaundice, breastfeeding‑failure jaundice, hemolytic causes, and rarer pathologic etiologies and will permit appropriate management decisions (observation vs phototherapy vs further workup).
